This research explores communication as an embodied process shaped by rhythm, perception, and presence. It focuses on subtle bodily signals that could influence dialogues before speech. The project introduces Seppia, a device that allows participants to perceive each other’s heartbeat in real time through sound. Rather than translating signals into data, it preserves their rhythmic quality, shifting interaction from interpretation to perception.

column3: What If Flowers Came From the Moon?
column6: This project begins with the observation that reflection tends to appear in the in-between moments, rather than in clearly defined events. It explores how these moments are shaped by time, environment, and attention, and how they contribute to personal change. Instead of producing reflection, it asks how space can be made for it to happen.
This paper examines how replication reinforces culture and knowledge democratization through a historical analysis of Romanian Principalities and digital realm.

column3: From Consumption to Digestion: Rethinking Engagement in a Contemporary Media Environment
column6: Fast moving media encourages us to consume information without processing it – without feeling nourished by it. This project uses digestion as a metaphor to rethink how we take in information.

column3: VISUAL AND LINGUISTIC PATTERNS IN HUNGARIAN POLITICAL COMMUNICATION: COMPARING THE 1950S SOCIALIST ERA TO TODAY'S GOVERNMENT MESSAGING
column6: This thesis examines parallels between Hungarian communist-era political communication (1945–1956) and that of the contemporary ruling party, Fidesz. The aim is to show how visual and linguistic patterns from that period are still present today. Growing up in Hungary, I witnessed this shift firsthand: in 2010, government messaging was barely visible; now every corner is covered in billboards repeating similar messages through a unified visual language. The research approaches this question from two directions — visual and linguistic.

Elena, classified as a "Mute" by a bureaucratic system, has applied 48 times over 18 years to regain her voice, only to be denied by an impossible architecture of standards designed to ensure failure—a denial delivered by the system's own aware operator, Castellan, and witnessed by the indifferent Archive worker who processes the paperwork. Told through three interlocking voices, the narrative exposes how institutional violence operates through procedure and how bureaucratic denial becomes indistinguishable from design, with an author's confessional afterword that grounds the speculation in historical reality.

This essay examines how perfume functions as a carrier of memory, desire, and loss through the myth of Eden. Drawing on psychology and philosophy, it argues that scent operates as a trigger for nostalgia, making absence physically perceptible. Through research and collaborations with perfumers, the project reframes fragrance as a way to engage with decay, time, and the impossibility of return.

column3: The Echo of an Unshared Mind
column6: This project explores the relationship between hyper-awareness, isolation, and perceptual distortion through a narrative essay structured in three movements. It follows Tristan, initially accompanied by a psychologist, to examine how excessive self-perception, first experienced as control and precision, gradually destabilises his ability to remain oriented within reality. In Paris, hyper-awareness is constructed as a heightened sensitivity to social space. Tristan constantly perceives himself within situations, anticipating gestures, correcting speech, and adjusting his presence. This produces a doubling, where a “second Tristan” observes and evaluates the first. What appears as precision progressively turns inward, becoming continuous self-surveillance. The transition to isolation unfolds through the journey to the castle. As external interactions diminish, the friction that previously grounded perception disappears. Tristan’s awareness no longer adjusts to others, but expands without resistance. In the castle, this process intensifies. The space remains stable, yet small discrepancies accumulate: echoes extend, reflections lag, and repeated actions become absorbing. Observation begins to precede experience, as notes describe Tristan before he acts. The distinction between observing and being observed collapses. This culminates in the emergence of a presence following him, initially ambiguous, then revealed as his own image, misaligned and delayed. What appears as an external threat is inseparable from his own perception. The project constructs a perceptual trajectory through the essay, later translated into film. It suggests that the risk lies in excess, when perception folds inward and can no longer distinguish between what is produced and what is perceived.

This work explores the tension between skateboarding and the city. It examines how urban spaces are designed, experienced, regulated, reclaimed by skateboarders, and how cities and skateboarding engage in a dialogue to shape public space. ?Heterotopia?? The physical location of utopia that harbours the imagination. That is what the dialogue between skate and the city is today. Perhaps it also involves proposing new forms (whether skateable or not) for public space…

column3: The World of the Instinctive Being

column6: Command Z explores how digital, mechanical, and manual methods of making shape the design experience, particularly in relation to time, decision-making, and errors. Through reproducing the same text across a laptop, typewriter, and letterpress, it examines how each medium affects pace, control, and the reversibility of actions. Drawing on theories by Franco Berardi and Walter Benjamin, it argues that tools fundamentally reshape the temporal structure of design work and reveal tensions between optimisation and acceptance in creative practice.

column3: Trust the MESS: A queer guide to failing fabulously
column6: How can failure and non-mastery function as methods for knowledge production and connection in a society shaped by over-optimisation??Maybe the answer is already in the process. Less outcome. More trying. Repeating. Failing again.

column3: Monsters, Plebs and Freaks at the Periphery
column6: Romania wants to be too much like the West, and the Boys will make that happen. They will buy the lands, they will build the churches, they will cut the woods, and they will launder the money. They will be elected mayor for 20 years in a row; they will be corrupt. This work examines Pipera, a peripheral district in northern Bucharest, where corporate modernity and balkanism converge. Drawing on phenomenology, self-colonisation, and monster theory—through the frameworks of Sara Ahmed, Maria Todorova, Alexander Kiossev, and Jeffrey Jerome Cohen—alongside auto-theory, the essay poetically contextualises and reframes Pipera’s transformation from village to Corporate Horror, positioning the Corporation™ as a contemporary monster. The work raises questions about what it means for a seemingly modern periphery to remain symbolically marginal while simultaneously producing new peripheries of its own. The writing moves fluidly between a poetic and an academic voice, while deliberately subverting conventional punctuation and academic writing norms as a way of hijacking concepts of sterility explored throughout the essay.

column3: De Toko: Between Shelf and Street
column6: A visual essay that questions what happens when the toko disappears, and how it creates belonging through everyday routines and encounters. Through personal memory and a recorded maternal interview, it reflects on what remains when culture moves beyond the places that once held it.

column3: Synthetic Transcendence: To what extent can AI-generated images interpret a person’s emotional and spiritual experience of everyday life?
column6: Synthetic Transcendence explores the extent to which AI-generated images can interpret a person’s emotional and spiritual experience of everyday life. In my practice, I utilize image-making in the form of photography and text-to-image generation to unravel the tension between ‘real’ and ‘fake’ images. Inspired by my Australian-Chinese upbringing in Singapore’s ‘expat bubble’, I aim to shed light on this less obvious culture and community that I grew up with. Through applications of Susan Sontag’s ‘The Aesthetics of Silence,’ John Berger’s ‘Ways of Seeing,’ Lev Manovich’s ‘AI Aesthetics’, and Masahiro Mori’s ‘Uncanny Valley,’ I examine how AI-generated images mystify and challenge our perception of reality. I comment on the intentions of my own image-making project, photographer Daniel Vaysberg’s work, and Midjourney's founder David Holz’s philosophy, exploring outcome fundamental theories of visual meaning in effect. This research exploration concludes that text-to-image generation is a cure for the desire to visually clarify mental concepts, that AI-generated images confront current assumptions about contemporary art, and that they can be harnessed as beacons to procure personally meaningful creations rather than a deceptive performance.

column3: Women–Poetry–Translation: Rewriting Feminist Voices across Text and Archive
column6: How do women’s voices travel across language, image, and history? This project moves through Korean feminist poetry and publication archives from the 1980s and 1990s, tracing how women’s lives have been written, visualised, and circulated. It brings translation and archival materials into conversation, not as separate domains, but as intertwined forms of feminist expression. By placing poems alongside images, it asks how feminist histories can be read differently — and how translation might open new ways of seeing what has not yet been fully visible.

column3: queer indie publishing manifesto: making a case for (making) queer zines
column6: this web-zine presents a glimpse into the world of queer independent publishing, namely self-published analogue zines. the research behind this text has sparked from the feeling of personal frustration with the corporate graphic design world, and is fuelled by the hope to find meaning and community within alternative publishing practices. queer indie publishing manifesto plays with the idea of individual vs. collective authorship by weaving together words of many people from the field.

column3: The Seaside Towns That Forgot to Close Down
column6: ‘The Seaside Towns That Forgot to Close Down’ is a photographic project that draws on a narrative of visible decay and socio-economic struggle throughout English seaside towns; the project captures familiar seaside features such as piers, promenades or arcades, while drawing attention to signs of deterioration, manifested as rusted structures, fading facades, and rotting materials.

What if we start seeing the city as a stage? That a red light, a crossing, a line can function as stage markings? What if people are not just passing by, but performing? Public space is usually understood as a functional environment designed to organise movement and behaviour. Roads for traffic, markings for order, getting from A to B. But I'd like to invite you to see that differently. Where road markings, crossings, traffic lights, and unwritten social conventions form spatial scripts that direct how people move, wait, and adjust to one another. This visual essay asks: how can framing high-traffic public spaces through the camera transform everyday movement into choreography?

Struggling Writing investigates writing as a material, performative, and temporal practice that resists transparency, asking what becomes possible when writing becomes unstable, resistant, and materially present rather than functioning as a neutral tool. Drawing on Siyahmashq (dense Persian calligraphic practice), Adorno's essay as form, Henry Corbin's imaginal realm, and Federico Campagna's prophetic world-making, the research treats illegibility, hesitation, and breakdown as productive conditions explored through hand-drawing, creative coding, type design, and typographic system-building. This text articulates the conceptual, theoretical, and methodological framework of an ongoing practice-led research project, while the final work takes two forms in conversation: a printed visual essay and a web-based typographic environment, both using typefaces designed during the research. The work translates written arguments into typographic conditions where meaning redistributes across rhythm and density, and the struggle of writing becomes perceptible as material encounter.

When the idea of home becomes an invisible, intimate realm, no longer tied to a structural or geographical location, the objects we collect along our way, made, created, and taken, become a way for us to fold up and pocket our metaphorical homes. Our spiritual home—the one that lives within our minds, or rather, our body. Through playing with the idea of living within our memories and experiences, we find different ways to enter the home, thus questioning what it means to be at home, or what home can be when living in a world of metaphor.

column3: Unclaiming all bad energy! Claiming good energy. Claim x 4. Claim with good energy only!
column6: This essay explores the relationship between social media algorithms and folklore, arguing that contemporary digital platforms function as a modern form of myth-making. While folklore once spread through oral storytelling and later through images and print, belief today circulates through algorithmic repetition and personalised media environments. Using the example of the 1934 “Surgeon ’ s Photograph” of the Loch Ness Monster alongside contemporary experiences of algorithmically driven content, the essay examines how repetition, emotional response, and the illusion of meaning transform coincidence into belief. Drawing on media theorists such as Marshall McLuhan, Vincent Mosco, Valentina Tanni and Tommaso Venturini, the essay situates social media within a longer history of technological media reshaping how truth is produced and experienced. Particular attention is given to the concept of the digital sublime, in which algorithms are experienced not simply as tools but as powerful and mysterious systems that appear to reflect and shape reality itself. Through a combination of TikTok comments, theoretical analysis and personal reflection, the essay argues that in an era of information overload and emotional media, superstition has not disappeared but has instead evolved into a new form of digital folklore sustained by algorithmic culture.

column3: Carrying the Force of a Poem
column6: I am drawn to writing that resists a single forward line and instead moves through interruption, repetition, tonal shift, juxtaposition, and return. What interests me is how these formal qualities can be carried beyond the text itself: how layout can support the movement of a poem on the page, how publishing can shape the conditions under which it is met, and how circulation can help create stronger and wider connections between poetry and its readers.

The project began from my personal experience as a Korean student reading in a second language and developed through three operations: marking, transforming, and accumulating. column3: A polished System and its remains

column6: This essay exists as a séance. As an act of forming a memory of the unfamiliar, and an exploration of presence — how it finds a way to reveal itself without its author, storyteller or original context. The process of printing, scanning, framing, zooming in, taking apart and putting together again. In itself, as much a tool as an emerging method of storytelling. Creating a coherent narrative that sequentially finds its way through scattered dishes, ghostly embraces and posed rows of glaring eyes, planting a feeling of familiarity in the unfamiliar.

This research explores how pre-defined structures, particularly grids, influence image-making and authorship. Instead of starting from a blank surface, it investigates what happens when creation begins within an existing framework. Through experiments, workshops, and artist dialogues, it examines how grids shape decisions, repetition, and variation. The project reveals authorship as a shared process, where creative agency emerges through interaction between maker and structure rather than individual control.

column3: I don't seem to care enough about sourdough to stand in line.
column6: This research explores how gentrification in The Hague is transforming craft culture, shifting it from an inclusive practice into a more commercial and identity-driven phenomenon associated with the “Havermelkelite.” Through fieldwork and theory, it examines the tension between authentic and performative craft in contemporary urban spaces.

This paper understands itself as an exhausted sigh in the long-known, holding what’s uncomfortable to see. Out of a desire for more caring ways of being, I collect and gradually combine moments of interaction between us and our non human kin.

What does it mean to write and read numbers? I try to encourage a more associative way of looking at graphic design, reminding the importance of borrowing, tracing and re-contextualising forms in the field of typography.
